name: Pictish
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: We have no good or conclusive evidence for the position of the accent in Pictish (but see below). [p. 28] ... The position of the stress accent in Pictish cannot be established with any confidence, as the available evidence provides no unambiguous indications of its location. [...] The polysyllabic Pictish loanwords in Gaelic (bagaid & monadh) have initial stress, as one would expect in this language, masking whatever may have been its original position. [...] This change only occurs after the accent so this indicates that the development was broadly as follows /moˈnijo-/ > /moˈniðjo-/ > /moˈnið/. This would suggest that, as with Brittonic, the stress lay on the penultimate at this period. However, caution is required [p. 29]
new_statements.citation: Rhys, Guto. 2015. Approaching the Pictish language: historiography, early evidence and the question of Pritenic. PhD thesis, University of Glasgow.
new_statements.locator: Section 'The Accent', pp. 28-29 (PDF pp. 29-30); cf. fn. 665, p. 329 (PDF p. 330)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The author states that the position of word stress in Pictish cannot be determined: all evidence (king-lists, place-names, loanwords) has passed through initial-stress languages (Gaelic, Scots/English). One loanword, Gaelic monadh, whose /j/ > /ð/ change is accent-conditioned, tentatively suggests penultimate stress on the pre-apocope form (as in Brittonic); fn. 665 notes that after Pictish apocope this syllable would be final, and whether stress later shifted to the penult is uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: Koch's derivation of Itharnan from *isarno- would require initial stress in Roman-period 'Pictish', but the author rejects that etymology (derives the name from Latin Aeternus), so it is not counted as evidence.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct language known only from names (king-lists, place-names, ogham inscriptions) and a few loanwords into Gaelic; the statement concerns the word accent of Pictish as reconstructed from these, and the author deliberately leaves the accent unmarked throughout the thesis. The tentative penult hint refers to the pre-apocope stage.
new_statements.identity_note: The source treats Pictish (pict1238) as the language of the medieval Pictish name evidence and discusses separately a putative Roman-period 'Pritenic' stage; the accent statement covers Pictish proper and no differently named variety. The Glottolog 'grammar/phonology' count is 0; the language is extinct and known only from onomastic and inscriptional fragments.

sources.locator: Section 'The Accent', pp. 28-29 (PDF pp. 29-30); cf. fn. 665, p. 329 (PDF p. 330)
sources.note: Section 'The Accent' (pp. 28-30): no good or conclusive evidence for the position of the accent in Pictish; it 'cannot be established with any confidence'; the Gaelic loanword monadh (/moˈnijo-/ > /moˈnið/, /j/>/ð/ only after the accent) hints that stress lay on the penult as in Brittonic, with caution; fn. 665 (p. 329) adds that after Pictish apocope the accent would then lie on the final syllable and that any later shift to the penult is uninvestigated; accent deliberately left unmarked in the thesis.
